A sine current has I_m = 10 A. Its rms value is

Rule: I_rms = I_m / √2.
Apply: 10 / 1.414 = 7.07 A.
Check: 14.1 A multiplies instead of dividing, 6.37 A is the half-cycle average (2 I_m / π), 5 A is half the peak.
A sine wave has V_m = 50 V. Its average value over a half cycle is

Rule: V_avg = 2 V_m / π ≈ 0.637 V_m.
Apply: 0.637 × 50 = 31.8 V.
Check: 35.4 V is the rms value, 70.7 V is V_m × √2, 25 V is half the peak.
i = 5 sin(ωt + 90°) A and v = 20 sin ωt V. The current
is in phase with the voltage

Rule: φ = ψ_v − ψ_i, and φ < 0 means v lags i.
Apply: φ = 0° − 90° = −90°, so the voltage lags the current: the current leads by 90°.
Check: Lagging needs φ > 0, in phase needs φ = 0°, opposite needs φ = ±180°.
Two sine waves of 50 Hz are 60° apart. The time difference between them is

Rule: time shift = (φ / 360°) × T.
Apply: T = 1 / 50 = 20 ms, so (60 / 360) × 20 ms = 3.33 ms.
Check: 1.67 ms belongs to 30°, 6.67 ms to 120°, and 20 ms is one full period.
Which phasor represents v = 30 sin(ωt − 40°) V (peak values)?

Rule: a peak phasor has the magnitude V_m and the angle ψ.
Apply: V_m = 30 V and ψ = −40°, so V = 30∠−40° V.
Check: 30∠40° has the wrong sign of the angle, 30√2 would be an rms-to-peak mix-up, and −30∠40° changes both.
